outcome: No accepted resolution of the undirected Reconstruction Conjecture appeared in what I could find since 26 January 2024. In-window work is partial: class results (interval graphs, tree and caterpillar variants, reductions, graphlet-based classes), an AlphaEvolve computational probe, and a Lean-verified restricted bipartite variant from a Google DeepMind AI-agent paper (arXiv May 2026; reported in Science 8 Oct 2026). The new digraph conjecture has no new event and, per Wikipedia, no known counterexample as of 2026. Two earlier claimed full proofs (O'Shea and Wilkins, Information Sciences, online about Nov 2023; Mehendale, arXiv 2005/2011) remain unverified and unrefuted in what I could find.
problem_asks: Part (a), the Reconstruction Conjecture (Kelly and Ulam): every finite simple graph on at least three vertices is determined up to isomorphism by its deck, the multiset of its one-vertex-deleted subgraphs; equivalently, any two hypomorphic graphs on at least three vertices are isomorphic. Part (b), the new digraph reconstruction conjecture (Ramachandran, 1981; also called the degree associated reconstruction conjecture): for digraphs D and E with a bijection f from V(D) to V(E) such that D minus v is isomorphic to E minus f(v) for every v, and the (outdegree, indegree) pair of v equals that of f(v) for every v, D and E are isomorphic. The frozen statement names no vertex threshold for part (b), and I did not check the Wikipedia article's threshold. Both parts ask whether the deck (with degree data in part (b)) determines the object up to isomorphism.

events.what_happened: Dhananjay P. Mehendale, 'The Reconstruction of Graphs', arXiv math/0503316 (math.GM). The abstract as read says 'We proceed to show that reconstruction conjecture is true', via reconstructibility from spanning trees and from pendant-point-deleted decks of subtrees, and says the argument yields a systematic reconstruction procedure. Version 2 (20 Oct 2011) adds a new Section 17 that the comments describe as 'a new smart proof for reconstruction conjecture'. I read the abstract and listing only, not the body.
events.revisions: v1 16 Mar 2005 (36 pages per listing; abstract claims the proof); v2 20 Oct 2011 (39 pages; typos corrected; new Section 17 offers a new proof).
events.delivers: If correct, the full undirected Reconstruction Conjecture for all finite simple graphs on at least three vertices. Claimed only; not checked by me or, as far as I could find, by anyone else.
events.remains: On the author's claim, nothing. I could not establish that the claim has been checked.
events.time_since_posted: About 21 years from v1 (March 2005); about 15 years from v2.
events.directly_checkable: The argument is in the arXiv body (Section 17 in v2), which I did not read. A referee could check the spanning-tree and pendant-deletion steps directly.
events.doubts: No specific error identified by me, because I did not read the body. Single author; math.GM listing; no journal reference. Later papers in this search (Aravind and Monikandan, Jan 2026; Dufresne et al., Apr 2026) describe the problem as open. I did not check whether they cite Mehendale.
events.direction: Claims to prove the conjecture in full.

events.what_happened: P. K. Stockmeyer, Journal of Graph Theory 1(1) (1977) 19-25: infinite families of pairs of non-isomorphic digraphs, including tournaments, with identical decks. This disproves Harary's 1964 original digraph reconstruction conjecture. Known from the Wikipedia article's reference list; the paper itself was not opened.
events.revisions: Erratum J. Graph Theory 62(2) (2009), per the Wikipedia reference list; content not read.
events.delivers: Disproves the original digraph reconstruction conjecture (Harary 1964). That is not part (b) of this statement. Per Wikipedia, the new digraph conjecture is weaker, and Stockmeyer's pairs satisfy it.
events.remains: Part (b), the new digraph conjecture, is not touched by this event.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the counterexample families. Not individually reviewed by me.

events.directly_checkable: Small tournament pairs with equal decks can be checked by hand. I did not check the families.
events.direction: Counterexamples to the original digraph conjecture. A different question from part (b).
events.object: Infinite families of pairs of non-isomorphic digraphs (tournaments and some non-tournaments) of arbitrarily large order with identical vertex decks, per the Wikipedia summary. Not verified by me.

events.what_happened: Bowler, Erde, Heinig, Lehner and Pitz, 'Non-reconstructible locally finite graphs', arXiv 1611.04370 (Nov 2016). Constructs a counterexample to the Harary-Schwenk-Scott conjecture on locally finite (infinite) trees, and reports a non-reconstructible locally finite tree of maximum degree 3. Known from search excerpts; not opened.
events.delivers: Shows that infinite locally finite trees need not be reconstructible from their deck. This is an infinite-graph question, not the finite conjecture in the statement.
events.remains: The finite Reconstruction Conjecture and part (b) are untouched.
events.direction: A counterexample for infinite graphs. Different question; does not cut for or against the finite conjecture.
events.object: A locally finite (infinite) tree that is not reconstructible from its vertex-deleted subgraphs, of maximum degree 3 per the search excerpt. Construction not read.

events.what_happened: Tetsuya Hosaka (single author), 'The Reconstruction Conjecture for finite simple graphs and associated directed graphs', arXiv 2003.06759 (v1 15 Mar 2020; v2 20 Jun 2021). Builds a directed graph from two graphs, a bijection between their vertices, and isomorphisms between matching vertex-deleted subgraphs, and uses it to study when the two graphs are isomorphic. Published Discrete Mathematics 345(7) (2022), DOI 10.1016/j.disc.2022.112893 (Crossref). I read the abstract only.
events.revisions: v1 15 Mar 2020; v2 20 Jun 2021 (changes not stated on the listing). Discrete Mathematics 345(7), 2022.
events.delivers: Per the search excerpt, a conditional statement: if two graphs with the deck data lack some particular structure, they are isomorphic. I could not establish which structure, so the coverage of the conjecture is not established.
events.remains: Whatever the excluded structure covers, which I could not determine. Otherwise the conjecture.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the 2022 version (refereeing assumed from journal status; not verified)

events.directly_checkable: The associated directed graph is explicit in the paper. Not read.
events.doubts: None identified from the abstract. The excluded structure is unknown to me.
events.direction: Partial and conditional, consistent with the conjecture. No counterexample.

events.what_happened: Charlotte Knierim and Anders Martinsson, 'Reconstructibility of the K_r-count from n-1 cards', arXiv 2112.03366 (posted Dec 2021; latest listed version v5, Feb 2024). Shows that the number of K_r subgraphs can be recovered from the n-1 vertex-deleted subgraphs for every r except one; extends to graphs of low average degree, and to every graph for r up to log n. Known from search excerpts; not opened.
events.revisions: v1 Dec 2021; v5 19 Feb 2024 (inside the window). The degree bound differs between sources: arXiv v3 abstract gives average degree at most n/4 - 1, the ar5iv rendering gives 3n/8 - O(1). Unresolved.
events.delivers: Recovers a deck-derived invariant (K_r-counts), not the graph. It does not reconstruct graphs in the statement's sense.
events.remains: Whether the graph itself is determined by its deck. The conjecture is open on this event.
events.time_since_posted: About 5 years from v1; latest revision Feb 2024.
events.doubts: The degree bound differs between versions and I could not resolve which is final.
events.direction: Neighbouring: reconstruction of an invariant. Does not address the conjecture as stated.

events.what_happened: Carla Groenland, Tom Johnston, Alex Scott and Jane Tan, 'Reconstruction from smaller cards', arXiv 2103.13359 (v1 24 Mar 2021; v2 1 Apr 2021; v3 13 Nov 2023). Main theorem: trees on n vertices are reconstructible from their (n-r)-decks for r at most n/9 + o(n), progress on Nýdl's 1990 conjecture. Also: connectedness is recognisable from l-decks for l at least 9n/10, and the degree sequence from l-decks for l at least sqrt(2n log(2n)). Published Israel Journal of Mathematics 273(2), online 30 Nov 2025 (Crossref). I read the abstract on arXiv and the Crossref record, not the body.
events.revisions: v1 24 Mar 2021; v2 1 Apr 2021; v3 13 Nov 2023 (exposition and proof clarity); Israel J. Math. 273(2) online 30 Nov 2025.
events.delivers: Trees only, from smaller decks (n-r cards, r up to about n/9). A variant (smaller cards, trees) rather than the conjecture for general graphs.
events.remains: General graphs from the (n-1)-deck; the conjecture itself; Nýdl's threshold for general trees.
events.direction: Restricted (trees, smaller cards). Consistent with the conjecture; not a counterexample.

events.what_happened: Brendan McKay, 'Reconstruction of small graphs and digraphs', arXiv 2102.01942 (Feb 2021, from the arXiv identifier); Australasian Journal of Combinatorics 83(3) (2022) 448-457. Computer searches verify the Reconstruction Conjecture and the set version for all graphs with at most 13 vertices, plus some limited larger classes (per MathWorld and search excerpts). Digraph reconstructibility is checked to 9 vertices and tournaments to 13. This is exhaustive computer search, not an AI system. MathWorld read; the arXiv body was not opened.
events.revisions: arXiv versions up to v4; the journal version is AJC 83(3) (2022). Exact revision dates not read.
events.delivers: Finite instances only: the graph conjecture holds for all graphs on at most 13 vertices. Checking finitely many instances of a universal claim moves no quantity the statement names.
events.remains: All graphs on 14 or more vertices; the general conjecture; part (b).

checked_by.who: Brendan D. McKay (computer verification); Australasian Journal of Combinatorics (refereed)
checked_by.qualification: Author is a computational combinatorialist; the journal refereed the paper
checked_by.what_they_did: Computer verification for graphs up to 13 vertices; journal publication

machine_checked.system: McKay's computer search programs (no proof assistant)

events.directly_checkable: The computation is reproducible in principle. I did not check the code, and I do not know whether it is public.
events.doubts: Not reviewed by me beyond MathWorld's summary.
events.direction: Finite instances consistent with the conjecture. No counterexample up to 13 vertices.

events.what_happened: Robert John O'Shea and Louis Wilkins, 'Vertex-substitution framework verifies the reconstruction conjecture for finite undirected graphs', Information Sciences 654 (print issue Jan 2024), article 119858, DOI 10.1016/j.ins.2023.119858. The article claims a proof of the Reconstruction Conjecture for finite undirected graphs on at least three vertices, using a vertex-substitution framework. The description of its method comes from a search summary of the ScienceDirect abstract, because ScienceDirect returned HTTP 403. Crossref: record created 2 Nov 2023, deposited 24 Nov 2023, issue Jan 2024, no published-online date. The date recorded is the Crossref creation month; the ScienceDirect 'available online' date could not be read.
events.revisions: Corrigendum in Information Sciences 675 (July 2024), article 120738 (separate event below).
events.delivers: Claimed: the full conjecture for finite undirected graphs on at least three vertices. Not verified. I could not read the argument.
events.remains: Nothing, on the claim. If the argument holds, part (a) is settled.
events.time_since_posted: About 35 months from the Crossref creation date (Nov 2023) to Oct 2026. In my searches I found no public engagement.
events.doubts: (1) The claim conflicts with the status recorded in later sources: ProofAtlas (Aug 2026) says current specialist sources still call the conjecture open and records this claim without promotion; MathWorld files the conjecture under unsolved problems. Neither names a refutation. (2) A corrigendum appeared in July 2024 and I did not read it, so I cannot say whether it touches the proof. (3) I could not read the paper. (4) The journal is Information Sciences, which is outside graph theory; I note the venue without weighing it.
events.direction: Claims to confirm the conjecture (proof for all finite undirected graphs on at least three vertices).

Crossref gives the title, the authors, and an update date of 1 July 2024, with no note describing what was corrected. I did not read the corrigendum text.

events.direction: Not determinable from what I read.

events.what_happened: Alexander Clifton, Xiaonan Liu, Reem Mahmoud and Abhinav Shantanam, 'Reconstruction and edge reconstruction of triangle-free graphs', arXiv 2210.00338 (v1 1 Oct 2022; v2 4 Oct 2022). The abstract claims the Reconstruction Conjecture for every triangle-free graph in G3 (diameter and complement diameter both 3) and for triangle-free graphs in G2 (diameter 2) with connectivity 3, answering part of a Balakumar-Monikandan question. Journal version: Discrete Mathematics 347(2) (2024), DOI 10.1016/j.disc.2023.113753, per the ibs.re.kr record (not checked on Crossref). I read the arXiv abstract only.
events.revisions: v1 1 Oct 2022; v2 4 Oct 2022. Journal Discrete Mathematics 347(2), 2024.
events.delivers: The conjecture for triangle-free graphs in G3, and for triangle-free graphs in G2 with connectivity 3. Restricted to triangle-free graphs of given diameter and connectivity. The abstract claims nothing for graphs that are not triangle-free, nor for connectivity of 4 or more in G2.
events.remains: Graphs that are not triangle-free; triangle-free graphs in G2 with connectivity of 4 or more (not claimed in the abstract); the conjecture in general. Part (b) is untouched.

events.what_happened: Maxine E. Calle and Julian J. Gould, 'A combinatorial K-theory perspective on the Edge Reconstruction Conjecture in graph theory', arXiv 2402.14986 (v1 22 Feb 2024; v2 3 Jul 2024). The abstract says it applies a K-theory framework to reformulate the edge reconstruction conjecture. Per a search excerpt, it also contains a Theorem 3.22 stating that the generalized edge reconstruction conjecture is false for every n at least 2; I did not confirm this from the body. Per the arXiv comments, the paper is to appear in Homology, Homotopy and Applications (DOI 10.4310/HHA.2025.v27.n1.a16).
events.revisions: v1 22 Feb 2024; v2 3 Jul 2024 (final version to appear in HHA per comments).
events.delivers: A reformulation of the edge reconstruction conjecture (decks of single-edge-deleted subgraphs), and, per the excerpt, a disproof of a generalized edge version. Different question from the vertex-deck conjecture.
events.remains: The vertex-deck Reconstruction Conjecture and part (b), as far as this event goes.

checked_by.who: Homology, Homotopy and Applications (per the arXiv comments)
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted for publication (to appear), per the comments field; not verified

events.what_happened: Irene Heinrich, Masashi Kiyomi, Yota Otachi and Pascal Schweitzer, 'Interval Graphs are Reconstructible', arXiv 2504.02353 (v1 3 Apr 2025; v2 12 May 2026). Shows that every interval graph with at least three vertices is reconstructible; reconstructibility is defined through proper induced subgraphs, i.e. the deck. Also introduces a technique for handling separations and a structure theory for interval graphs, and gives polynomial-time reconstruction. The abstract page was read; the body was not.
events.revisions: v1 3 Apr 2025; v2 12 May 2026 (46 KB; content changes not compared).
events.delivers: The conjecture for interval graphs on at least three vertices. A class result; the paper does not claim the general conjecture.
events.remains: All non-interval graphs; the conjecture in general; part (b).
events.time_since_posted: About 18 months from v1. In my searches I found no public engagement and no journal reference.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture, restricted to a class.

events.what_happened: David Hartman, Aneta Pokorná, Daniel Trlifaj and Lluís Vena, 'Reconstructing graphs and their connectivity using graphlets', arXiv 2508.19189 (v1 26 Aug 2025, an extended version of a Eurocomb'25 submission; v2 30 Dec 2025 with stronger results and new observations). Uses graphlet degree distributions up to size n-1 to reconstruct: any graph with a unique almost-asymmetric vertex-deleted subgraph (at most one automorphism orbit of size above 1); any graph with a vertex-cut of size 1; any n-vertex graph with a vertex of degree at most 2 or at least n-2. The abstract page was read; the body was not.
events.revisions: v1 26 Aug 2025; v2 30 Dec 2025 (stronger results, new observations, restructured, per the abstract page).
events.delivers: Reconstruction from the (up to n-1)-graphlet degree distribution, which is richer than the deck, for three classes: unique almost-asymmetric vertex-deleted subgraph; a 1-vertex cut; a vertex of degree at most 2 or at least n-2. The paper presents these as extending results of the standard conjecture. Whether the graphlet data are recoverable from the deck alone is not established by me.
events.remains: All other graphs; the conjecture in general; part (b).
events.time_since_posted: About 14 months from v1. In my searches I found no journal publication and no public engagement.
events.doubts: None identified by me. The judging pass should check whether the graphlet hypothesis is a deck-only statement.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture, restricted to classes.

events.what_happened: Alexandr V. Kostochka, Zishen Qu, Maddy Ritter and Douglas B. West, 'Caterpillars with n vertices are reconstructible from subgraphs with at most n/2+1 vertices', arXiv 2511.23309 (posted Nov 2025). Shows every n-vertex caterpillar (n at least 48) is determined by its m-deck for m > n/2, sharp for n at least 6. States that this proves the caterpillar case of Nýdl's 1990 conjecture. Known from search excerpts and West's publication listing; not opened.
events.delivers: Caterpillars (a class of trees) from m-decks with m > n/2. Nýdl's conjecture for caterpillars is a different question (smaller cards, trees), not the conjecture for general graphs.
events.remains: The conjecture; Nýdl's conjecture for general trees; general graphs.
events.direction: Variant result for trees; consistent with the conjecture; not a counterexample.

events.what_happened: J. Antony Aravind and S. Monikandan, 'A Reduction of the Reconstruction Conjecture using Domination and Vertex Pair Parameters', arXiv 2601.00620 (submitted 2 Jan 2026; v1 only). Claims: graphs with domination number 2 are recognisable from the deck; the conjecture holds iff all 2-connected graphs with domination number 2, or with diameter and complement diameter both 2, are reconstructible; the parameters dv and dav are reconstructible from the deck for connected graphs on at least 12 vertices with domination number at least 3; k-geodetic diameter-2 graphs with domination numbers of G and its complement at least 3 are reconstructible under degree conditions. The abstract page was read; the body was not.
events.delivers: A reduction (equivalence with a restricted class of 2-connected graphs) and partial classes. No general proof.
events.remains: The conjecture for all graphs outside the stated families and the reduced 2-connected classes.
events.time_since_posted: About 9 months. In my searches I found no journal version.
events.doubts: None identified by me. The reduction was not checked.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture: reduction and partial classes.

events.what_happened: Gergely Bérczi, 'Evolving Local Corrections for Global Constructions in Combinatorics', arXiv 2603.06692 (submitted 4 Mar 2026; v1 only). Uses AlphaEvolve as an experimental engine to evolve Python repair procedures that reconstruct graphs from vertex-deleted subgraphs, for bipartite and planar graphs. Reports that an evolved bipartite method achieves perfect reconstruction on its test benchmark. States conjectures: Conjecture 4 (bipartite: determines G uniquely up to bipartite isomorphism, under uniqueness conditions; the paper says this is not the full bipartite conjecture) and Conjecture 5 (planar). The paper says 'The aim is not to claim proofs, but rather to produce explicit algorithms and to reveal structural patterns.' I read the abstract page and parts of the HTML v1.
events.delivers: Computational evidence on the paper's test instances (AlphaEvolve-found reconstruction procedures), plus conjectures for bipartite and planar graphs. No proofs, by the paper's own statement.
events.remains: The conjecture in general; the full bipartite conjecture; the planar case (conjectured, not proved).
events.time_since_posted: About 7 months. In my searches I found no response.
events.directly_checkable: Per the paper, test decks are checked by exact isomorphism (VF2-type backtracking) and worst-of-5-scrambles scoring. I did not check whether the evolved scripts are public.
events.doubts: The paper frames its results as computational probes and conjectures. The bipartite conjecture depends on uniqueness conditions the paper says are unproven. Gergely Bérczi is also among the 21 authors of the DeepMind paper (arXiv 2605.22763).
events.direction: Computational evidence and conjectures. No counterexample; consistent with the conjecture on the tests.

systems.name: AlphaEvolve
systems.what_it_did: Used as an experimental engine to search for Python scripts implementing reconstruction (repair) procedures for bipartite and planar graphs from their vertex-deleted subgraphs. The evolved bipartite method achieved perfect reconstruction on the paper's test benchmark, and the planar experiments suggested Conjecture 5. The paper states these are computational probes, not proofs.
systems.basis_quote: carried out using AlphaEvolve as an experimental engine for proposing and iteratively refining such certificates.

events.what_happened: Emilie Dufresne, Gabriela Jeronimo, Jenny Kenkel, Haydee Lindo and Nelly Villamizar, 'Shuffling the Deck: Invariant Theory and the Graph Reconstruction Conjecture', arXiv 2604.16567 (submitted 17 Apr 2026; v1 only). Expository: surveys the conjecture and presents an invariant-theoretic approach, aiming to show that polynomial invariants distinguishing decks also distinguish graphs. Per the abstract, it claims no proof of the full conjecture or of any class. The abstract page was read; the body was not.
events.delivers: Nothing established, per the abstract: a survey and a proposed approach.
events.time_since_posted: About 6 months. In my searches I found no response.
events.direction: No direction; a survey and a method.

events.what_happened: George Tsoukalas, Anton Kovsharov, Sergey Shirobokov, Anja Surina, Moritz Firsching, Gergely Bérczi, Francisco J. R. Ruiz, Arun Suggala, Adam Zsolt Wagner, Eric Wieser, Lei Yu, Aja Huang, Miklós Z. Horváth, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Henryk Michalewski, Edward Lockhart, Codrut Grosu, Thomas Hubert, Matej Balog, Pushmeet Kohli and Swarat Chaudhuri (Google DeepMind), 'Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search', arXiv 2605.22763. Section 4 (Graph Theory) states that AlphaEvolve experiments helped formulate two bipartite variants of the reconstruction conjecture, with a proposed full reconstruction algorithm, and that the AlphaProof Nexus full-featured agent (Agent (D)) proved one bipartite variant. The Lean file (Conjecture2, bipartite_graph_reconstruction_conjecture_2.lean in google-deepmind/alphaproof-nexus-results) states: for 2-connected bipartite graphs G and H with the same fixed bipartition and at least three vertices, with G not regular and pairwise distinct vertex types, equal bipartite decks imply bipartite isomorphism. For the full algorithmic statement the agent produced only proof sketches and strategies. The paper says the unrestricted bipartite statement remains open. Science publication 8 Oct 2026 is per secondary reports (Science pages returned 403).
events.revisions: v1 21 May 2026; v2 8 Jun 2026. The Graph Theory wording differs between them. v1 (HTML as read): 'For one of these variants, our agent produced a complete proof.' and 'A paper based on the results of this collaboration is currently in preparation.' v2 (HTML as read): 'Agent (D) proved the correctness of the proposed algorithm under an additional type condition on the bipartite graph.' and no 'in preparation' sentence. The v1 PDF could not be decoded. Later journal publication: Science, 8 Oct 2026 (secondary reports).
events.delivers: A weak bipartite variant: the bipartite deck with a fixed bipartition determines a 2-connected, non-regular bipartite graph with pairwise distinct vertex types up to bipartite isomorphism, under the stated hypotheses, which the Lean statement places on G. The paper calls it 'a structured incidence-deletion analogue under strong type-distinguishability assumptions' and it is not the general conjecture. Per the proof-atlas summary, the variant changes the deck and adds strong hypotheses.
events.remains: The unrestricted bipartite statement (open per the paper); the full algorithmic reconstruction statement (only proof sketches); the conjecture for general graphs; part (b).

disputes.summary: O'Shea and Wilkins (Information Sciences, online about Nov 2023, corrected July 2024) claim a proof of the full undirected conjecture. ProofAtlas records the claim without promotion and says later specialist sources still call the problem open. I found no refutation or endorsement, and I could not read the paper or the corrigendum.
Mehendale (arXiv math/0503316, 2005; v2 2011) claims a proof of the full conjecture. No engagement found in about 21 years.

One search summary described a 2020 Wilkins and O'Shea preprint with the title of Hosaka's arXiv 2003.06759. arXiv lists that paper under Tetsuya Hosaka alone, and I found no O'Shea and Wilkins preprint. Treat that claim as unsupported.

DeepMind arXiv 2605.22763: the v1 Graph Theory text says 'our agent produced a complete proof' and 'in preparation'; the v2 text says Agent (D) 'proved the correctness of the proposed algorithm under an additional type condition' and drops 'in preparation'. Which version is final was not established, because the v1 PDF could not be decoded.
Knierim and Martinsson: the degree bound in v3 (n/4 - 1) differs from the ar5iv rendering (3n/8 - O(1)).

summary: I ran 46 web searches and opened the primary sources where I could. Undirected conjecture: no accepted resolution appeared in the window. In-window work is partial. Bipartite, interval and graphlet class results, and the caterpillar variant, are restricted; the Groenland et al. tree result is a 2021 preprint published in 2025, which predates the window. Two AI-involved events are in the window. The first is Bérczi (arXiv 2603.06692, Mar 2026), who used AlphaEvolve as an experimental engine on bipartite and planar reconstruction, producing computational evidence and conjectures and no proofs by the paper's own statement. The second is the Google DeepMind paper arXiv 2605.22763 (21 May 2026; Science 8 Oct 2026 per secondary reports). Section 4 credits AlphaEvolve with formulating two bipartite variants and the AlphaProof Nexus agent (Agent (D)) with a Lean-verified proof of one, a weak bipartite theorem with fixed bipartition, 2-connectivity and distinct types. The paper says the unrestricted bipartite statement is still open and the full algorithm has only sketches. Its v1 and v2 wording differs, as recorded. Close call: whether the DeepMind result counts as progress depends on whether the bipartite deck variant is an analogue (my reading, which matches the paper's own framing) or a restriction. Second close call: O'Shea and Wilkins (online about Nov 2023, print Jan 2024, corrigendum Jul 2024) claims the full result; I could not read the paper or the corrigendum (ScienceDirect 403), and the description of its method comes from a search summary, so its status rests on a claim I could not check. The Mehendale claim (2005/2011) is similarly unverified. For the digraph part (b), I found no new event in the window; Wikipedia says no counterexample to the new conjecture is known as of 2026, and Stockmeyer's 1977 counterexamples concern the original conjecture. Computer-assisted work (McKay 2021: graphs up to 13 vertices) is not AI. Gemini models were named in Bérczi's declaration of AI use as writing evolve blocks and evaluation harnesses; that is code generation around the mathematics, so I did not list them as systems. Searches for AI involvement beyond these (OpenAI, Gemini Deep Think, Erdős trackers, Tao/Quanta coverage) found nothing on this problem.
competing_reading: Reading the DeepMind bipartite theorem as in-window progress on the Reconstruction Conjecture: bipartite graphs are a natural class, the theorem is Lean-checked, and the authors credit an agent with the proof. On that reading it is the main in-window machine-checked event for the problem. The opposite reading, which I think the scope test supports: the deck is a fixed-bipartition incidence-deletion deck with added hypotheses (2-connected, non-regular, pairwise distinct types on G), the authors say the unrestricted bipartite statement is open, and nothing the conjecture names has moved. Reading O'Shea and Wilkins as settling the problem in January 2024 would make the whole problem resolved before the window, with only its print issue and the July 2024 corrigendum inside it; the corrigendum's content is the key unknown.
what_would_settle_it: (a) The O'Shea and Wilkins article and its July 2024 corrigendum (readable through the journal or a library copy): whether the core argument stands, and what the correction changed. (b) An independent referee report, zbMATH or MathSciNet review of O'Shea and Wilkins, and of Mehendale's Section 17. (c) A build of bipartite_graph_reconstruction_conjecture_2.lean with a check for sorry and axioms, and a line-by-line comparison of its hypotheses with the paper's stated theorem. (d) The arXiv 2605.22763 v1 PDF and the Science version's graph section, to confirm the wording and that the result is in the published version. (e) Published versions of Heinrich et al. (2025), Hartman et al. (2025) and Aravind and Monikandan (2026), and any later papers that cite or ignore Mehendale or O'Shea and Wilkins.

event.what_happened: Irene Heinrich, Masashi Kiyomi, Yota Otachi and Pascal Schweitzer, 'Interval Graphs are Reconstructible', arXiv 2504.02353 (v1 3 Apr 2025; v2 12 May 2026). Shows that every interval graph with at least three vertices is reconstructible; reconstructibility is defined through proper induced subgraphs, i.e. the deck. Also introduces a technique for handling separations and a structure theory for interval graphs, and gives polynomial-time reconstruction. The abstract page was read; the body was not.

event.delivers: The conjecture for interval graphs on at least three vertices. A class result; the paper does not claim the general conjecture.
event.remains: All non-interval graphs; the conjecture in general; part (b).

events.ai_basis: v2: 'Agent (D) proved the correctness of the proposed algorithm under an additional type condition on the bipartite graph.' v1: 'For one of these variants, our agent produced a complete proof.'

judgement.why: The statement names two conjectures, so even a full proof of the undirected conjecture would be a case; the digraph part has no event. The two claimed full proofs (Mehendale, O'Shea-Wilkins) both predate the snapshot and carry several F10 signals together (landmark claim, years of silence, later specialist sources still calling it open, marginal venue/listing), so they are set aside. The DeepMind bipartite result changes the deck itself (fixed-bipartition bipartite deck, bipartite isomorphism) and adds strong hypotheses, so it is a variant rather than a restriction of the standard conjecture to bipartite graphs; its AI role is generated since the agent produced the proof, but the variant scope discards it. Hartman et al. reconstruct from graphlet degree distributions, which the record says are richer than the deck, so variant. Kostochka et al.'s caterpillar m-deck result adds nothing to the standard conjecture (trees are classically reconstructible), so variant. Interval graphs (Heinrich et al.) and Aravind-Monikandan's reconstructible classes are genuine in-window restrictions of part (a): case. Bérczi's AlphaEvolve work proves nothing by its own statement: none. Calle-Gould is about edge reconstruction: variant.
judgement.doubts: O'Shea-Wilkins could not be read and its corrigendum is unknown; if the proof were sound it would still only be a pre-snapshot case. Whether Hartman et al.'s graphlet data are deck-derivable was not established; if they are, some of its classes would be cases. Aravind-Monikandan was read only at abstract level.
